title: Gentiles: What Happened to Northern Kingdom?

sense.text:
This class goes into the beef Israel had among ourselves, going back to the beef between the Southern Kingdom of Israel and the Northern Kingdom of Israel, and what happened to both kingdoms, but primarily the Northern Kingdom. It’s important to learn the history of your people as thoroughly as possible, because the people who are not our people know more about our history than us, and that should not be the case.

Isaac told Jacob, “Thou shalt not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan.” Jacob was told by his father not to take upon him a heathen woman to wife. That was always the law, even before Moses.

“God Almighty bless thee, and make thee fruitful, and multiply thee”, “and give thee the blessing of Abraham, to thee, and to thy seed with thee”. The same covenant and blessing the Lord bestowed upon Abraham and Isaac was passed on to Jacob.

Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and charged him not to take a wife of the daughters of Canaan, and “that Jacob obeyed his father and his mother”. Esau had already gone and taken Hamite women, the women his parents told him not to marry. Then when he heard that Jacob got blessed and was sent to marry a woman of his own kind, he still went and married a heathen woman: he went to Ishmael’s children.

So Esau was a fornicator, a rebellious fornicator towards his parents. He did not obey his parents. He was evil and rebellious then, and he’s evil and rebellious now.

“Behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.” Jacob saw the gateway to Paradise. He was at the doorway of paradise; the Lord revealed it to him where he was.
“Behold, the Lord stood above it, and said, I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac”. This Lord that Jacob saw was Christ. He saw Christ there.

“Thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south”: the four corners. Over time, after King David and Solomon, we did explorations; we sailed the sea, especially during Solomon’s time, and we found ourselves migrating willfully into different lands, and we were heavily abundant in those lands. It began as willful migration, and based upon our wickedness it became forceful migration, captivity, in which we were scattered into all these four corners, prophetically.

“And in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed”: Christ will bless the families of Israel throughout the four corners of the earth.
“Thy name shall not be called any more Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name”. The Lord changed Jacob’s name to Israel.

God said to Israel, who was once Jacob, “I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee, and kings shall come out of thy loins”. Why is he saying a nation and a company of nations to Jacob? Jacob gave birth to one people, so why a nation and a company of nations? We’ll deal with that later on.
“Thou shalt have this son also”, because she already had Joseph. Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin: she called him “Ben–oni: but his father called him Benjamin.”

“Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father’s concubine”. Reuben was the firstborn. “Now the sons of Jacob were twelve”. Leah also had Dinah, a daughter. Jacob had twelve sons, and by the time of David all twelve tribes had pretty much become a kingdom: King Saul was set over them, then he died, and David came after him.

By this point David is anointed king, and there was the beef between Judah and the tribes of Ephraim. “Why have our brethren the men of Judah stolen thee away”: Ephraim, the Northern Kingdom, is asking Judah, why’d you take David from us? He’s our king too.
“Because the king is near of kin to us”: we’re the same tribe.

“We have ten parts in the king”: if you include Dan, that gives you ten; Dan eventually no longer became a tribe, they blended in with Benjamin. There’s more of us than you, we have more land than you. “We have also more right in David than ye”: we have more right to have David reign over us in our land than ruling over you in your land, even though he’s your tribe. He should be a king over us more than over you.

“And the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.” Judah pretty much cursed out the Northern Kingdom, and they fell back.

During this time there was no split. But over time a rivalry took place between Judah and Ephraim, a beef. That rift, that division, that hatred we had towards one another, was prevalent even when David was newly appointed king: division among the twelve tribes, Judah and Ephraim, Ephraim being Ephraim, Manasseh and the other tribes. Judah resided in the southern portion and Ephraim in the northern portion, thus the terms Southern Kingdom and Northern Kingdom. There was a hatred there, and it’s slightly spoken of in this context.

David’s son Solomon now begins to reign. “King Solomon loved many strange women”. The Zidonians are Canaanites. These are the nations “concerning which the Lord said unto the children of Israel, Ye shall not go in to them, neither shall they come in unto you: for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods”. The nations the Lord told Solomon not to deal with, and tells us not to deal with, Solomon dealt with anyway, and he ended up serving their gods.

“His wives turned away his heart after other gods”. Solomon sought to learn the ways of his heathen wives, the idolatry of his heathen wives.

“Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians”: that’s your Easter today. Ashtoreth was a fertility goddess: fertility orgies and indiscriminate sex, so you have sex with random people. “Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites”: that’ll be your Planned Parenthood today, Milcom the god of abortions. All of them are gods of abortions, but Milcom is primarily the one you read about involved in child sacrifice. Milcom and them were the destroyers of the babies that were made during the worship of Ashtoreth, spring to winter.
The Lord “had commanded him concerning this thing”: he told him not to do it, “that he should not go after other gods”.

“I will surely rend the kingdom from thee, and will give it to thy servant.” “Notwithstanding in thy days I will not do it for David thy father’s sake: but I will rend it out of the hand of thy son.” I’m not going to rend it out of your hand during your time, but in your son’s time I’m going to do it.
“Howbeit I will not rend away all the kingdom”: I won’t take away all the kingdom from you. “But will give one tribe to thy son for David my servant’s sake”: that be Benjamin.

The Lord said, I’m going to rip half of your kingdom out of your hand and give it to your servant. This is the servant right here: “Jeroboam the son of Nebat”, “Solomon’s servant”, “even he lifted up his hand against the king.” His servant tried to take Solomon out, to kill Solomon, and it’s going to explain why.

“Solomon seeing the young man that he was industrious, he made him ruler over all the charge of the house of Joseph.” Solomon saw that this man was smart, he was wise, so he set him up over the affairs of Joseph, the Northern Kingdom, Ephraim: the nine tribes, and if you count Dan, ten tribes.
“But I will take the kingdom out of his son’s hand”: Rehoboam’s hand.

The prophet Ahijah promised that Jeroboam would gain rulership over the ten tribes. A prophet told him, you’re going to gain rulership over your king’s kingdom. So Jeroboam, being hasty, rebelled against Solomon and tried to take Solomon out, tried to force it. That wasn’t the plan.

Jeroboam “was fled from the presence of king Solomon, and Jeroboam dwelt in Egypt”. He fled from Solomon because he tried to take Solomon out and Solomon tried to kill him for it. So he ran to Egypt, and while he was in Egypt, in Shechem they made Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, king.

“Thy father made our yoke grievous”. When Solomon began to worship and serve the gods of his wives, he built high places and houses for his wives. That cost money and resources, and he put heavy taxes on the people; he put those burdens upon the people. So they said, if you want us to serve you, all you got to do is take off the heavy burden your father put on us serving these heathen wives of his, “and we will serve thee.” A very simple, very basic task.

“Depart yet for three days”: give me three days, I’ll think about it. “King Rehoboam consulted with the old men, that stood before Solomon his father while he yet lived”: the elders that were around during his father’s time, obviously wise men that counseled Solomon, who was a wise man. He had advisors: “How do ye advise that I may answer this people?”
“If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever.”

“But he forsook the counsel of the old men”. This dude was an idiot. Rather than listen to the elders, he listened to his boys, his childhood friends he grew up with. He got counsel from his childhood friends rather than his father’s counselors and advisors: yo, yo, my man, what do you think I should do about the people and their request?

“My little finger shall be thicker than my father’s loins.” I’mma be harder on you; I’m going to be a bigger and rougher man on you than my father was. They gave him disrespectful counsel: usurp your authority, let them know that you run things, you’re the king now. They counseled him to be even harder on the people. “My father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions”: don’t cross me, I’m the king now, you’re going to do what I say.
The third day shows up, and “the king answered the people roughly, and forsook the old men’s counsel”: your father was hard on you, I’m going to be harder on you.

“Wherefore the king hearkened not unto the people; for the cause was from the Lord, that he might perform his saying, which the Lord spake by Ahijah the Shilonite unto Jeroboam the son of Nebat.” The Lord moved his spirit to listen to the stupid young men he grew up with rather than the elders. That was all the Lord’s plan. This stupidity of his was done to cause the prophecy Ahijah gave Jeroboam to be fulfilled, that he would reign over a portion of Israel. It had to play out this way, otherwise Ahijah’s prophecy would be void. The Lord used Rehoboam, who was an idiot, to forsake the counsel of the old men and cause a bigger division than there already was in 2 Samuel 19:41.

“What portion have we in David?” If that be the case, if you won’t listen to us, why should we deal with y’all? What portion do we have in your rulership? “Neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse”: we ain’t dealing with David no more. “To your tents, O Israel”: we out, we leaving, we gone. “Now see to thine own house, David”: from now on you’re going to rule over Judah, deal with Judah; we’re going to do our own thing.

That’s the beef now between the two. That beef was already around in 2 Samuel 19 when David was newly appointed king; now it’s solidified and confirmed, even worse, because of Rehoboam’s actions, all by the Lord of course. Judah, you do you; Ephraim, we going to do us.

The split took place in verse 16. Highlight it, underline it, put a bullet point there. The division was already present in 2 Samuel 19:41-43; the split officially took place in 1 Kings 12:16. Put those together.

“But as for the children of Israel which dwelt in the cities of Judah, Rehoboam reigned over them.” Judah and Ephraim shared land; Judah and Simeon, for example, were in the same land mass. So Simeon was subject to Rehoboam’s rule even though they weren’t dealing with Judah no more. Any group of the Northern Kingdom that shared the land with Judah was under Rehoboam’s rule.

Rehoboam “sent Adoram, who was over the tribute; and all Israel stoned him with stones, that he died.” He sent the tax collector to get taxes from the Northern Kingdom, and they threw stones and killed him. “So Israel rebelled against the house of David unto this day”: unto the time this was written, which was long after.

“There was none that followed the house of David, but the tribe of Judah only.” Judah only, but you also have Benjamin: Rehoboam “assembled all the house of Judah, with the tribe of Benjamin”, so you know it wasn’t just Judah. Benjamin was a fierce tribe, and the Lord left Benjamin with Judah; that’s that light right there. Rehoboam’s plan was to rise up Benjamin and Judah and take Ephraim back under his rulership by force, to regain the kingdom from Jeroboam, because the Northern Kingdom anointed Jeroboam their king according to the prophecy of Ahijah the prophet.

“Ye shall not go up, nor fight against your brethren the children of Israel: return every man to his house; for this thing is from me.” Leave them alone. I caused this division, because of what Solomon did.
“Jeroboam built Shechem in mount Ephraim”. Keep that word Shechem in mind; it’s important later on. He built there a place of worship for the Northern Kingdom.

“If this people go up to do sacrifice in the house of the Lord at Jerusalem, then shall the heart of this people turn again unto their lord, even unto Rehoboam king of Judah, and they shall kill me”. The main place to worship was the temple in Jerusalem. Jeroboam’s fear was that if they returned and worshipped at the temple among Judah, they would desert him and go back under Rehoboam. He couldn’t let that happen, because of that beef, that division.

“The king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem”. These golden calves are idols going back to Egypt, to the calf god there. Rather than go to the temple and worship, your gods are right here: “behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.” This guy was an idolater. He lived in Egypt when he fled from Solomon, so obviously he learned of the gods while he was there, the gods we worshipped when we were there before Moses took us out of Egypt, and he brought them right back to us again. He set one in Bethel and one in Dan.

“He made an house of high places, and made priests of the lowest of the people, which were not of the sons of Levi.” He made the low lives, the basest of the Northern Kingdom, priests. He fired Levi from their priestly duties, damn, and set up the Northern Kingdom instead.

“Jeroboam ordained a feast in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, like unto the feast that is in Judah”. This dude made new gods and made up his own holidays. This is pretty much an ancient Kwanzaa. Rather than keep the feast over there, you’re going to keep the feast here and honor these gods here, on the same day as the feast day of the Lord, which is Tabernacles. He made up his own feast day based on Tabernacles, like what black folks do with your Christmas and your New Year: we make the customs of the heathen our own. This guy gave us fake gods and a fake holiday behind the gods, “even in the month which he had devised of his own heart”: he made it up in his head.
Write this down: the book of Kings primarily focuses on the Northern Kingdom of Israel and its kings; the book of Chronicles primarily focuses on the Southern Kingdom of Israel and its kings.
“Ye shall not go up, nor fight against your brethren: return every man to his house: for this thing is done of me.” We just read this in 1 Kings 12. The same thing is being repeated.

The Levites had no portion of land or inheritance. Their inheritance was the priesthood, and they had portions of land in the suburbs of all the twelve tribes, did sacrifices for the people and taught them the laws throughout every tribe. But Jeroboam set up idols in calves and raised the lowest of the people as priests instead. So if the lowest of the people are the priests now, what happens to Levi? “The priests and the Levites that were in all Israel”, in all the Northern Kingdom’s suburbs, “resorted to him out of all their coasts”: they ran to Rehoboam.

“For the Levites left their suburbs and their possession, and came to Judah and Jerusalem: for Jeroboam and his sons had cast them off from executing the priest’s office unto the Lord”. The Levites were fired from the Northern Kingdom.
“He ordained him priests for the high places, and for the devils”: the devils are the golden calves, “and for the calves which he had made.” Same thing: idols.

“And after them out of all the tribes of Israel such as set their hearts to seek the Lord God of Israel came to Jerusalem”. After them, from the Northern Kingdom: not all of the Northern Kingdom followed or worshipped those golden calves. Some of them kept on returning to Jerusalem to worship. Not all of Ephraim was wicked as hell. Some of them said, this is evil as hell, we’re going to worship in Jerusalem. Not all of them fell for the two golden calves, but most of them did.

“So they strengthened the kingdom of Judah”: Levi strengthened Judah. The Southern Kingdom first consisted of Judah and Benjamin; now it consists of Judah, Benjamin and Levi. Write that down: Judah, Benjamin and Levi is the Southern Kingdom. Ephraim and the rest, the other nine, Ephraim, Manasseh, Reuben, Zebulun, Asher, Gad, is the Northern Kingdom. Don’t sit here stupid; you’re going to get confounded. You got to be paying attention here.
“In the twenty and seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel began Azariah son of Amaziah king of Judah to reign.”

He became king at sixteen and “reigned two and fifty years in Jerusalem”: fifty-two years. “He did that which was right in the sight of the Lord”: Azariah was a righteous king. Keep in mind he reigned for fifty-two years, and he began to reign during the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam.

precepts.why:
Write this down too. “Then all the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in the room of his father Amaziah.” Wait a minute: I thought it was Azariah? Azariah and Uzziah are the same person, different name, same king. Uzziah is the most popular name; Azariah is the other name given to him in Kings.

The details line up with 2 Kings 15: “Sixteen years old was Uzziah when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty and two years in Jerusalem.” “And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his father Amaziah did.”

So this is King Uzziah, and that’s the name to use: he began to reign at sixteen, he reigned fifty-two years, and Jeroboam was in the twenty-seventh year of his ruling.

sense.text: “In the thirty and eighth year of Azariah king of Judah did Zachariah the son of Jeroboam reign over Israel in Samaria six months.” Remember Uzziah reigned fifty-two years, so in his thirty-eighth year Zachariah reigned over the Northern Kingdom in Samaria, for six months. Why six months?
“He did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, as his fathers had done”. The Northern Kingdom had not one good king, not a single one. Every last one of them was evil and stupid.

“Shallum the son of Jabesh conspired against him, and smote him before the people, and slew him, and reigned in his stead.” He took over. You had mutiny, constant mutiny, in the Northern Kingdom, numerous times.

Shallum began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah, “and he reigned a full month in Samaria.” This dude reigned one full month, “for Menahem the son of Gadi went up from Tirzah, and came to Samaria, and smote Shallum”, slew him and reigned in his stead.

When you shed blood, you’re going to die by it. You live by the sword, you die by the sword. That goes for us too, even here in Philly, Chicago, Cali: these Negroes be killing each other, killing people, and they’re constantly looking over their shoulder, because they killed mad people and they’re going to be killed the same way. That hatred we have for each other has been around for thousands of years: murdering each other, you murder me, I murder you, you kill my mom, I kill your mama. It’s nothing new. Thousands of years of hatred against hatred, blood against blood, bloodshed.
“Then Menahem smote Tiphsah”, “and all the women therein that were with child he ripped up.” He was killing babies, cutting the womb open and ripping babies out.

“In the nine and thirtieth year of Azariah king of Judah”: still Uzziah. Uzziah reigned straight for fifty-two years, and the Northern Kingdom went through three kings in that time. Menahem began to reign because he killed Shallum, and “reigned ten years in Samaria”: he got a little bit of grace, ten years.
“He departed not all his days from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin.” He worshipped the same golden calves; they all did.

“And Pul the king of Assyria came against the land”, against Ephraim. Write this down: Pul is Tiglath-pileser the Third; Pul is short for his name. Pul was an Assyrian king.

“Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver, that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom in his hand.” Menahem paid the Assyrian king tax to make sure he stays ruler, stays reigning over the land.

Menahem exacted the money of the mighty men of wealth “to give to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria turned back, and stayed not there in the land.” Assyria left him alone and didn’t overthrow him.

“In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah Pekahiah the son of Menahem began to reign over Israel in Samaria”. Remember Uzziah reigned fifty-two years; at the fiftieth year Pekahiah is reigning over the Northern Kingdom, and Menahem is gone.

“But Pekah the son of Remaliah, a captain of his, conspired against him”: Pekahiah’s own captain conspired against him, smote him in the palace of the king’s house, killed him and reigned in his room.
“In the two and fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah Pekah the son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria”: the fifty-second year, the last year of Uzziah’s reign.

“In the days of Pekah king of Israel came Tiglath–pileser king of Assyria”: the same Pul we read about earlier, same guy, the Third. He took Gilead, Galilee and “all the land of Naphtali, and carried them captive to Assyria.” This is the first wave. The first wave of the Northern Kingdom being deported out of the land and taken into Assyria was right here; it was done in waves. Pekah began to reign in the fifty-second year of Uzziah, and Pul conquered the Northern Kingdom at this time.

precepts.why: That’s the first wave; it was done in waves. “Beerah his son, whom Tilgath–pilneser king of Assyria carried away captive: he was prince of the Reubenites.” So he took portions of Reuben away also.

“And the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgath–pilneser king of Assyria, and he carried them away, even the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh, and brought them unto Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and to the river Gozan, unto this day.”

sense.text: “Ahaz the son of Jotham king of Judah began to reign” “in the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah”. Uzziah had Jotham, and Jotham had Ahaz. “Twenty years old was Ahaz when he began to reign, and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, and did not that which was right in the sight of the Lord his God, like David his father.”

“But he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, yea, and made his son to pass through the fire, according to the abominations of the heathen, whom the Lord cast out from before the children of Israel.” Ahaz started falling into the ways of the northern kingdom, doing what they were doing. “And he sacrificed and burnt incense in the high places, and on the hills, and under every green tree.”

“Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to war”. When Ahaz was going into his idolatry, Pekah and Rezin got together and made an alliance to go against Judah, because by this time Judah’s going the hell off.

“And they besieged Ahaz, but could not overcome him.” They could not overcome him because the Lord defended Judah. Isaiah 7 is where this same history is repeated in more detail.

The same history as 2 Kings 16, in more detail: “in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah”, “Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up toward Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it.”

“Syria is confederate with Ephraim. And his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind.” The Lord sends Isaiah with his son to meet Ahaz: “Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands”, “Because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah, have taken evil counsel against thee”. These two, Syria and Ephraim, conspired together to overthrow Judah.

“Let us go up against Judah, and vex it, and let us make a breach therein for us, and set a king in the midst of it, even the son of Tabeal”. Syria and Ephraim got together to overthrow Judah and put a king over it, the son of Tabeal, to reign over all of us. “Thus saith the Lord God, It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass.”

“For the head of Syria is Damascus”: Syria’s capital was Damascus. “And the head of Damascus is Rezin”: the ruler over Damascus, over Syria, is Rezin.

“And within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.” Within 65 years Ephraim will be broken, that it shall not be a people. Underline that, highlight that verse: not a people. It is read multiple times in this class.

precepts.why:
“They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God; they have provoked me to anger with their vanities: and I will move them to jealousy with those which are not a people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.”

In this song Moses is prophesying of the split of Israel, the division between the Southern Kingdom and the Northern Kingdom, between Judah and Ephraim, before the twelve tribes were ever divided at all. “Not a people” in this verse is making reference to the northern kingdom: the same Ephraim that Isaiah says shall be broken, “that it be not a people.”

Keep these terms in mind, because they come back again: not a people, a foolish nation.

sense.text:
“Within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.” “And the head of Ephraim is Samaria”: Ephraim’s capital was Samaria. Shechem and Samaria are synonymous; keep that word in mind. “And the head of Samaria is Remaliah’s son”: the leader, the king of Samaria, was Remaliah’s son, Pekah.

“If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established.” Ahaz was afraid that these two were going to come together and overthrow him, because he was a wicked, faithless, evil king.

“Ask thee a sign of the Lord thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above.” “But Ahaz said, I will not ask, neither will I tempt the Lord.” So now he wants to be righteous: now he won’t tempt the Lord. “Hear ye now, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also?”

“Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign”. Verse 14 is very important to understand: this sign is twofold.

“Behold, a virgin shall conceive”: behold, a young woman of marriageable age shall conceive, that’s all it’s saying. “And bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel”, which means God with us. Verse 14 is alluding to Christ.

“Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good. For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings.”

By the time this child is born and knows good and evil, these kings will be gone: Rezin will be gone, and Ephraim will be broken, that it’s not a people. For a child to know to refuse the evil and choose the good, he has to be of a pretty good age, at least 10 or 11.

“The Lord shall bring upon thee, and upon thy people, and upon thy father’s house, days that have not come, from the day that Ephraim departed from Judah; even the king of Assyria.” He is going to raise up Assyria against these two. “The Lord shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria”: he is going to bring Assyria against these two kings, Ephraim and Syria.

Remember Isaiah 7:14: a virgin shall conceive and bear a son. Now: “Take thee a great roll, and write in it with a man’s pen”. Maher-shalal-hash-baz is the longest name of a person in the Bible, and it means quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil. Syria and Ephraim will be quick to the plunder and swiftly spoiled by Assyria.

Isaiah’s other son is Shearjashub, in Isaiah 7:3, which means a remnant shall return. His sons’ names were signs of prophecy yet to come to pass. This son is a sign that Assyria would overthrow these two kings.

“And I took unto me faithful witnesses to record, Uriah the priest, and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah. And I went unto the prophetess”: he went unto the prophetess to be his wife. “And she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the Lord to me, Call his name” Maher-shalal-hash-baz.

“For before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria.” This sounds like Isaiah 7:14-16. Isaiah’s child is already born, and before it has knowledge to cry my father and my mother, Damascus and Samaria are spoiled by Assyria.

Does a child that can’t say mommy and daddy know good and evil? No. It’s an age difference: this child is younger, so it’s two different kids. One prophecy is alluding to a future Messiah, and the other is referring to Isaiah’s kid.

Isaiah 7:14-16 is Messianic prophecy: a child being born, symbolizing deliverance from our captivity, from the oppressor, the Messiah being born proving that God’s with us in the future. Isaiah’s son, with that long name, is also a sign of deliverance from the oppressor during this time: Assyria not overthrowing them, meaning God is with us in Isaiah’s time. It’s parallel, but it’s not the same. When you quote Isaiah 7:14 about Christ, it wasn’t referring to this time; it’s referring to that time, our time now really.

“Forasmuch as this people refuseth the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah’s son; Now therefore, behold, the Lord bringeth up upon them the waters of the river, strong and many, even the king of Assyria, and all his glory: and he shall come up over all his channels, and go over all his banks”. His banks is Ephraim.

“And he shall pass through Judah; he shall overflow and go over”: he passes through Judah because he conquers Judah also. But “he shall reach even to the neck”: he won’t fully overthrow us. If you’re in the water and your head’s above the water, you’re not fully submerged. We won’t be drowned out by Assyria; Judah will be spared.

“And the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel.” Why is he saying O Immanuel? We didn’t get fully conquered; it was only to the neck. And what proves that God was with us in this chapter is Isaiah’s son, the one with the long name in verse 3. That son proves our deliverance from Assyria. That’s why it says God with us.
“Associate yourselves, O ye people, and ye shall be broken in pieces”, “gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces”: Ephraim and Syria.

“Take counsel together”: Syria and Ephraim. “And it shall come to nought”: it will not be successful. “Speak the word, and it shall not stand”: you will not conquer Judah and put a king up there, the son of Tabeal. That’s not going to happen. “For God is with us.”

And what proves that? Isaiah’s son proves it: they will be quick to the plunder and swiftly spoiled by Assyria, based upon Isaiah’s son being a sign. The children are the sign, not the woman.

precepts.why:
“For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings.” Set it beside Isaiah 8:4, “before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother”, and see the difference.

It’s very simple: the child in 7:16 will have knowledge of good and evil, but the other child won’t even have the knowledge to cry. That tells you the child in 8:4 is younger. It’s two different kids, meaning one prophecy is alluding to a future Messiah and the other is referring to Isaiah’s kid.

Before the child of 7:16 shall know good and evil, these kings are already gone; they’ll no longer be in existence. That is future. Verse 14 is alluding to Christ.

“And Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah the son of Remaliah, and smote him, and slew him, and reigned in his stead, in the twentieth year of Jotham the son of Uzziah.”

Pekah died within a year: before the child could say mommy and daddy. That is the fulfilling of Isaiah 8:4.

Ahaz began to reign and “did not that which was right in the sight of the Lord his God”, and “Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to war: and they besieged Ahaz, but could not overcome him.” Isaiah’s son being born proved that wasn’t going to happen.

“At that time Rezin king of Syria recovered Elath to Syria, and drave the Jews from Elath”. So Ahaz sent messengers to the king of Assyria, saying, “I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria, and out of the hand of the king of Israel, which rise up against me.” And Ahaz “took the silver and gold that was found in the house of the Lord, and in the treasures of the king’s house, and sent it for a present to the king of Assyria.”

“And the king of Assyria hearkened unto him: for the king of Assyria went up against Damascus, and took it, and carried the people of it captive to Kir, and slew Rezin.” He killed Rezin. So both of them got killed within a very short time, before the child could say father and mother. Historically they were conquered and overthrown within a year, because God was with us, based upon Isaiah’s son being born.

sense.text: “In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah began Hoshea the son of Elah to reign in Samaria over Israel nine years.” Hoshea conspired against Pekah and killed him, and now he’s king. “And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord”, of course he did evil, “but not as the kings of Israel that were before him.”

“Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria”: this is Shalmaneser the fifth, Pul’s son or grandson. “And Hoshea became his servant, and gave him presents.”

“And the king of Assyria found conspiracy in Hoshea: for he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and brought no present to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year”. Ephraim tried to ally itself with Egypt, who was a powerhouse at the time. Rather than give honor or pay tribute to Assyria, they decided to pay tribute to Egypt instead. “Therefore the king of Assyria shut him up, and bound him in prison.”

“Then the king of Assyria came up throughout all the land, and went up to Samaria, and besieged it three years.” Shalmaneser comes up and besieges Ephraim. This is the second wave. The first wave was in the days of Pekah, when the king of Assyria took Reuben and Naphtali, in 1 Chronicles 5:6 and 26.

“In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes”: Iran, upper Iran.

“The children of Israel had sinned against the Lord their God, which had brought them up out of the land of Egypt”, “and had feared other gods, And walked in the statutes of the heathen”. “And the children of Israel did secretly those things that were not right against the Lord their God”. Israel was doing wicked evil behind closed doors that they thought the Lord could not see.

Oftentimes among ourselves we get involved in wickedness and think he don’t see it, but he sees it all: the adultery, the lust, the murder, the hatred, the murmuring, the complaining. Ephraim was doing wickedness publicly and secretly, and God saw it all. When there’s hatred amongst each other, when brothers come in with hatred or anger towards their brother or their sister instead of loving them as yourself, the Lord sees it. Evil speaking toward each other, he sees it, he doesn’t like it, and he will overthrow you when you do that.

“And they set them up images and groves in every high hill, and under every green tree: And there they burnt incense in all the high places, as did the heathen whom the Lord carried away before them”, “For they served idols, whereof the Lord had said unto them, Ye shall not do this thing.”

“Yet the Lord testified against Israel, and against Judah, by all the prophets, and by all the seers, saying, Turn ye from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes”. Both Judah and Israel had prophets sent to them during the reign of these kings: Isaiah, Hosea, Micah, all these we call Minor Prophets, sent to prophesy against them for all the evil they were doing. And they were not listening, the northern kingdom first and the Southern Kingdom following after. “Notwithstanding they would not hear, but hardened their necks”.

“And they followed vanity, and became vain, and went after the heathen that were round about them, concerning whom the Lord had charged them, that they should not do like them.” Do not follow the other nations and their customs: Christmas, New Year’s, Thanksgiving, Halloween, birthdays. Don’t follow the other nations. But we choose to follow vanity and become vain and get destroyed.

That’s why oftentimes at the get-togethers and getaways the seats will be empty: “the children of Israel did secretly those things that were not right”. They’re out there with their family and friends eating turkey and opening up gifts; that’s why they ain’t in the room, not in the school. You got the day off, but you mysteriously had things to do that day.

“And they left all the commandments of the Lord their God, and made them molten images”, “and made a grove, and worshipped all the host of heaven, and served Baal. And they caused their sons and their daughters to pass through the fire, and used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the Lord, to provoke him to anger.”

“Therefore the Lord was very angry with Israel”: very angry with Northern Kingdom Israel. “And removed them out of his sight: there was none left but the tribe of Judah only.”

Be very mindful of this scripture, because people try to pick a doctrine out of it, that only Judah was left. It’s referring to the Southern Kingdom: “Judah only” means Judah, Benjamin and Levi were not removed out of their land. Ephraim was, by the Assyrians. The next verse proves it.
“Also Judah kept not the commandments of the Lord their God, but walked in the statutes of Israel which they made.” The Judah of verse 18 is the same Judah in verse 19: the Southern Kingdom.

“And the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel”: the northern kingdom. He “delivered them into the hand of spoilers”, the Assyrians, “until he had cast them out of his sight.”

“For he rent Israel from the house of David; and they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king: and Jeroboam drave Israel from following the Lord, and made them sin a great sin”: worshipping devils of golden calves. “For the children of Israel walked in all the sins of Jeroboam which he did; they departed not from them”; they stayed on worshipping those gods, “Until the Lord removed Israel out of his sight”, until the Lord removed the northern kingdom out of his sight, “as he had said by all his servants the prophets”, who prophesied against them before it took place and while it took place. “So was Israel carried away out of their own land to Assyria unto this day.”

“And the king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel”. He deported the northern kingdom out of the land and put heathens in the land.

That was Assyrian policy, like how America is: remove a people out of their land and place them in lands they have power over, to remove their sense of nationality from them. If you remove people from their land, they eventually begin to lose sight of who they are and where they come from. The Assyrians were the first to push the whole policy of heathen assimilation: put heathens in our land and put us in a foreign one, so we would lose all sense of national pride and identity.

“And so it was at the beginning of their dwelling there, that they feared not the Lord”. The heathens that lived there did not fear our God; they didn’t know our God, he ain’t their God. “Therefore the Lord sent lions among them, which slew some of them.”

“The nations which thou hast removed, and placed in the cities of Samaria, know not the manner of the God of the land”. There were certain things you had to do in order to be in our land. They didn’t belong there; these were imposters, squatters. While they lived in our land doing evil, God started killing them, and they went to the king of Assyria asking what to do while falsely occupying the land.

“Then the king of Assyria commanded, saying, Carry thither one of the priests whom ye brought from thence”: go get one of those low-level priests and bring him back, “and let him teach them the manner of the God of the land.” So they brought northern kingdom priests back in to teach them the sacrifices, so they could remain falsely occupying the land. One of the priests “came and dwelt in Beth–el, and taught them how they should fear the Lord”: what they should sacrifice, the dos and don’ts of living in the land.

“Howbeit every nation made gods of their own”. Even in the midst of sacrificing to our God in order to remain in the land falsely, they started their own gods, because our God was not their God.

Like today you got the Israelis saying that they’re Israel, but they don’t follow the God of the Bible. They follow a god that lets them put their mouths on baby penis; they’re in Brooklyn digging tunnels with baby clothes and bloody mattresses everywhere; they’re doing sex trafficking with our people in Guatemala, caught recently with a sex trafficking ring going on in Central America and South America. They do the bare minimum, like the heathens did here.

“And put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made”. The Samaritans were our people that resided in Samaria; Samaritans is another term for the northern kingdom, Ephraim. You will not find anywhere in the Bible where Samaritan is in reference to other nations, ever, though Christians are saying it and stupid Israelites are saying it too. The Samaritans were the original inhabitants of the land before the nations named in verse 24, and in verses 30 and 31, were put there.

Shalmaneser dies, and his relative, some say his brother, some say a cousin, takes over after him and does the same thing. “In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it”. Tartan was Sargon’s captain or commander.

Sargon reigned right after Shalmaneser, of the same royal family, and historically he finished what Shalmaneser did not complete. He was the last wave of removing the northern kingdom out of the land and placing them in the Assyrian areas, the cities of the Medes, around 722, 721 BC. Shalmaneser and Sargon were around the same time frame, one a little after the other, and one finished the other’s job of deporting our people into foreign lands.

Out of Sargon came the king who attacked Judah, and the angel came and killed all his men, 185,000 of them to be exact.

“Then they came to Zerubbabel, and to the chief of the fathers, and said unto them, Let us build with you: for we seek your God, as ye do; and we do sacrifice unto him”. These are they whom the king of Assur brought into the land; he did the same thing.

“But Zerubbabel, and Jeshua, and the rest of the chief of the fathers of Israel, said unto them, Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God; but we ourselves together will build unto the Lord God of Israel, as king Cyrus the king of Persia hath commanded us.”

“And Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city, even in Jerusalem: but they brought him not into the sepulchres of the kings of Israel: and Hezekiah his son reigned in his stead.” Ahaz died, and now his son begins to reign. You had Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and now you have Hezekiah.

“Hezekiah began to reign when he was five and twenty years old, and he reigned nine and twenty years in Jerusalem.” “And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father had done.” Hezekiah was a righteous king.
“He in the first year of his reign, in the first month, opened the doors of the house of the Lord, and repaired them.” In his very first year he opened the house of the Lord back up.

“And Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah, and wrote letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh, that they should come to the house of the Lord at Jerusalem, to keep the passover unto the Lord God of Israel.” Hezekiah reached out to the northern kingdom, to Ephraim and Manasseh, to come keep the passover at Jerusalem.

The posts went “throughout all Israel and Judah”, saying, “Ye children of Israel, turn again unto the Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, and he will return to the remnant of you, that are escaped out of the hand of the kings of Assyria.” So even after those kings of Assyria came through and deported the northern kingdom, Ephraim still remained: remnants of them remained in the land, and Hezekiah wrote to them.

“And be not ye like your fathers, and like your brethren, which trespassed against the Lord God of their fathers, who therefore gave them up to desolation, as ye see.” Remember, these men escaped Assyria overthrowing them.

“For if ye turn again unto the Lord, your brethren and your children shall find compassion before them that lead them captive, so that they shall come again into this land”. If you turn to the Lord, the Most High will grant you mercy while you are in the lands where your families were taken captive. “For the Lord your God is gracious and merciful, and will not turn away his face from you, if ye return unto him.”

“So the posts passed from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh even unto Zebulun: but they laughed them to scorn, and mocked them.” He sent these posts to the country of Ephraim, Manasseh and Zebulun, and that means Ephraim was still in the land even after those deportations. There were remnants of them left in the land. But this particular group spoken of in verse 10 was rebellious.
“Nevertheless divers of Asher and Manasseh and of Zebulun humbled themselves, and came to Jerusalem.” Nevertheless, despite verse 10, they came to do what? To worship.

“For a multitude of the people, even many of Ephraim, and Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not cleansed themselves, yet did they eat the passover otherwise than it was written.” So it wasn’t just Asher and Manasseh: it was Asher, Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun and Issachar that came.

“But Hezekiah prayed for them, saying, The good Lord pardon every one That prepareth his heart to seek God, the Lord God of his fathers, though he be not cleansed according to the purification of the sanctuary.” “And the Lord hearkened to Hezekiah, and healed the people.” They were healed from their impurities; Hezekiah prayed over them.

That goes right back to 2 Chronicles 11, where after Jeroboam’s priests, out of all the tribes of Israel such as set their hearts to seek the Lord God of Israel came to Jerusalem to sacrifice. There are remnants of Ephraim that were not displaced, that remained faithful to going to the temple. A perfect example of that is Tobit: when Ephraim was still in their land, before he got dragged into Assyrian captivity to the place of the Medes, he was still going up and offering sacrifices.

“And all the congregation of Judah, with the priests and the Levites, and all the congregation that came out of Israel, and the strangers that came out of the land of Israel, and that dwelt in Judah, rejoiced.” The strangers: the northern kingdom was called strangers. They left their land to come into their brother’s land to keep the passover, which made them estranged. So the northern kingdom in the Old Testament is called strangers. Keep that in mind; that’s very important to remember.

This is before Hezekiah, in the time of another righteous king. “And the Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded”: this Azariah is not the king, this is a prophet. He said to Asa and all Judah and Benjamin, “The Lord is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you.”

“Now for a long season Israel hath been without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law.” Without a teaching priest because they got rid of the priests; they kicked them out. And without law. Keep that in mind: that statement is written somewhere else.

“And he gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers with them out of Ephraim and Manasseh, and out of Simeon: for they fell to him out of Israel in abundance, when they saw that the Lord his God was with him.” The strangers with them: Asa gathered them out of Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon. King Asa reigned around 913 to 873 BC (BC goes backwards). So Ephraim was still in the land even after the onslaught.
“And he ordained him priests for the high places, and for the devils, and for the calves which he had made.” These are the golden calves Jeroboam put there.

“And after them out of all the tribes of Israel such as set their hearts to seek the Lord God of Israel came to Jerusalem, to sacrifice unto the Lord God of their fathers.” Out of all the tribes of the northern kingdom. Some of the northern kingdom always resorted back to keeping the laws of God, despite the golden calves Jeroboam put there.

Jeremiah is prophesying against Judah. “Therefore will I do unto this house, which is called by my name, wherein ye trust”: this house is referring to the southern kingdom; it’s referring to the temple. “And unto the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I have done to Shiloh.” Shiloh is the northern kingdom. So what I am going to do to this house, the southern kingdom, the temple here, is the same thing I did to Shiloh. What the Lord says he did to the northern kingdom he is now going to do to the southern kingdom.

“And I will cast you out of my sight, as I have cast out all your brethren, even the whole seed of Ephraim.” I cast all of them out; I’m going to cast all of you out. The same thing he said he would do to Judah, he already did to Ephraim. What he did to Ephraim with Assyria, he would do to Judah with Babylon.

“In his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant three years: then he turned and rebelled against him.” He rebelled against the king of Babylon, and so he gets taken into captivity and his son takes over.

“Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months.” He was evil as hell: “And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his father had done.”

“At that time the servants of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against Jerusalem, and the city was besieged.” The same way Assyria besieged the northern kingdom, Babylon besieged the southern kingdom.

“And he carried away all Jerusalem, and all the princes”: all the princes goes into Daniel and Ezekiel and them. “None remained, save the poorest sort of the people of the land.” So very few of the remnant remained; the poorest sort remained in the land.

Remember, the Lord said in Jeremiah, I’m going to cast all of you out the same way I did Ephraim. Yet here the poorest remained in the land, meaning remnants of Judah remained in the land during the Babylonian displacement, just as remnants of Ephraim remained in the land during the Assyrian displacement.

“The word of the Lord that came unto Hosea, the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel.” During the times of these kings, the kings we read about earlier, Hosea is prophesying against the northern kingdom.

“Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel.” He is going to overthrow the house of the northern kingdom, and that is Assyria. “I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.”

“Call her name Lo–ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away.” Remember, Isaiah’s son Mahershalalhashbaz was an ensign for deliverance; Hosea’s children were an ensign for captivity and destruction. Jezreel represents Israel, the seed of Israel, and Lo-ruhamah means no mercy for the house of Israel: no mercy for the northern kingdom.

“But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and will save them by the Lord their God, and will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by battle, by horses, nor by horsemen.” Assyria came up against the southern kingdom and got destroyed. What Assyria did to the northern kingdom they would not do to the southern kingdom.

“Call his name Lo–ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.” The Lord said, not only will I not have mercy upon you, you will not be my people and I will not be your God. Remember, Isaiah said they will be broken, that they be not a people.

So if you’re not God’s people and he’s not your God, what does that make you? Not a people. The northern kingdom became strangers, Gentiles, heathens: not a people, not God’s people, no mercy, no God. That’s heathens. Keep that in mind.

“Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom”. The book of Ezra is the Persian captivity: Cyrus of Persia comes into power and grants Israel the liberty to return to the lands they were displaced from, from both Assyria and Babylon.

“Then rose up the chief of the fathers of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests, and the Levites, with all them whose spirit God had raised”. With all them: the remnant of the northern kingdom. “To go up to build the house of the Lord which is in Jerusalem.” So you know that not all of the northern kingdom was displaced out of the land.

When this liberty was given to us to return to our lands, that beef, that division we had with each other, was still there. But remnants of the northern kingdom from the time of King Asa and Hezekiah, the ones who remained in the land, would still often come up to Jerusalem to sacrifice, and they came and helped us rebuild. The same way the Lord said he would cast out all of Ephraim and then cast out all of Judah too but left behind a remnant (Jeremiah 7:14-15), the Lord did not cast out all of both kingdoms. Remnants of them remained in the land.

precepts.why: “And after them out of all the tribes of Israel such as set their hearts to seek the Lord God of Israel came to Jerusalem, to sacrifice unto the Lord God of their fathers.” Out of all the tribes of Israel: the same thing as “all them whose spirit God had raised” in Ezra 1:5. That is the remnant of the northern kingdom that kept coming up to Jerusalem, and here they come up again with Judah, Benjamin and the Levites to build the house of the Lord.

sense.text:
The majority of the northern kingdom came to this side of the world: men like Hannibal and the Carthaginians were northern kingdom, men like El Tarif who crossed to Spain and conquered Spain during the Dark Ages were northern kingdom. The northern kingdom was also taken over to areas like China and Japan. Not all of the northern kingdom is on this side of the world, but the bulk of them are, and the remnants of that bulk are everywhere else; the same way the bulk of Judah was brought to this side in slavery and their remnants are everywhere else.

“Those are the ten tribes, which were carried away prisoners out of their own land in the time of Osea the king, whom Salmanasar the king of Assyria led away captive, and he carried them over the waters, and so came they into another land.”

“But they took this counsel among themselves, that they would leave the multitude of the heathen, and go forth into a further country, where never mankind dwelt, That they might there keep their statutes”. Why? Because Ephraim eventually stopped keeping them: they started going off into idolatry, cutting hearts out, building all kinds of sun temples. “Which they never kept in their own land.”

“And they entered into Euphrates by the narrow passages of the river. For the most High then shewed signs for them, and held still the flood, till they were passed over. For through that country there was a great way to go, namely, of a year and a half”. They passed through the Euphrates and made their way around the bottom of Africa, around the Cape of Good Hope, and from around Africa to the Americas is a year and a half. There’s a book brought out before about a slave who told his grandson it took him a year and a half to get to this side of the world.

“And the same region is called Arsareth”: another land, America, the land where never mankind dwelt. This land was uninhabited; that’s why it’s called the New World. The world everyone inhabited, Noah’s three sons, was called the Old World. None of Noah’s sons were on this side of the world; we got over here, and then the sons came over. No one else was here aside from us. Arsareth is America.

During the time of Persia, Israel was granted the liberty to return to their lands, but the northern kingdom, because of that hatred they had for us, the bulk of them said the hell with that, we’re going to go somewhere else.

The history book read in class shows it. In the days of Solomon, nearly 3,000 years ago, the Phoenicians, or Tyrians as they were then called, were ‘the only seamen of the age capable of conducting the fleets of Solomon’. Solomon was in contact with a king named Hiram, and they did business on the Indian Ocean together. Modern scholars say the Phoenicians were Canaanites, but the Phoenicians were our people: the Romans renamed Canaan Phoenicia, so the inhabitants of that land were called Phoenicians. That was us. Solomon’s fleet was us, and Solomon’s fleet and our people sailed to this side of the world; we knew about this side of the world already. The Phoenician sailors were men of Solomon; on board their fleets were ‘both Jews and Tyrians’, the same people.

The fleet that returned once in three years made voyages to the Atlantic. Solomon’s fleet traversed two oceans: the Indian is one and the Atlantic is the other. Ancient writers speak of a large and delightful island or land the Phoenicians discovered in the Atlantic Ocean west of Spain, which goes back to America. In the Atlantic west of Africa the regular trade winds are constantly blowing to the west. Even if a storm rips off your sails and your boat is just floating there, the wind will carry it westward no matter what. So any fleet that sails from West Africa will always end up on American shores, and fast.

Various kinds of coin have been found among the Native Americans. The ones the Europeans gave them when they colonized are little effaced by time and rust. But those brought here ‘by the first settlers from Asia’, meaning the East (scholars know the Native Americans sailed here from the East), are much more defaced because they’re older, and are of a very different stamp from the white man’s stamp: ‘some of these have the old Persian stamp’. Why do Native Americans have Persian-stamped coins? Because they just came from that land, from their captivity. In Ezra 1 Cyrus the king of Persia gave us leave to go back and rebuild Jerusalem, which Babylon destroyed. Persia gave us the funds and the ability to rebuild: those who returned from Assyria and from the Babylonian exile lands. Judah returned to Jerusalem, remnants of Ephraim returned and helped rebuild Jerusalem, and the bulk of Ephraim came here.

‘There can be but one answer to this question’: they must have been brought here by the first settlers, who must have had communication with the ancient Persians, ‘and what people except the Phoenicians and Jews had intercourse with the Persians at so remote a period’? So the Native Americans had to have been Phoenicians or Jews: the same people. Y’all better pay attention; you’re going to be out there teaching, and if you get confounded it’s going to be your fault.

Remember “not a people”: it’s in Deuteronomy 32:21, it’s in Isaiah 7 and 8, broken that it be not a people. “There be two manner of nations which my heart abhorreth”: the writer says there are two nations my heart cannot stand, I hate them. “And the third is no nation”: no nation, which is not a people. Two of them he hates, and the third is not a people.

“They that sit upon the mountain of Samaria”: the Greeks, because the Greeks took over Samaria. Write that down: those that sit upon Samaria, put a parentheses and put Greeks. “And they that dwell among the Philistines”: Hamites. He despised those two nations; they were always our mortal enemies.

“And that foolish people that dwell in Sichem.” Sichem is a Latinized version of the word; it is Shechem, the capital of Ephraim. That foolish people is the northern kingdom.

In verse 25 he says they’re no nation, not a people. Why? Because they would be broken, based upon Isaiah 7:8.

precepts.why:
“They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God; they have provoked me to anger with their vanities: and I will move them to jealousy with those which are not a people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.” Those which are not a people, a foolish nation: the same words as Ecclesiasticus 50, the foolish people that dwell in Shechem. That is talking about the northern kingdom.

So even after all those kings of Assyria came through, remnants of Ephraim remained in the land, and they were still stupid; that is the foolish people of Shechem.

sense.text: This goes to those that sit upon the mountain of Samaria. “Not long after this the king sent an old man of Athens to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers, and not to live after the laws of God”. The king here is Antiochus Epiphanes, and he sent his right-hand man.

“And to pollute also the temple in Jerusalem, and to call it the temple of Jupiter Olympius”: he defiled the temple in Jerusalem in Judah and called it the temple of Jupiter Olympius, or Zeus Olympius.

“And that in Garizim, of Jupiter the Defender of strangers”. Garizim is Shechem, Samaria: the place of worship in Samaria was made the temple of Jupiter the Defender of strangers, because you had Ephraim and heathen there. Remember Ephraim was called strangers, and they had strangers living among them in their land. “As they did desire that dwelt in the place”: the northern kingdom was still prone to idolatry, along with the heathens living in their land with them.

When they fought against the Greeks, we gained some power and authority. “At that time young Antiochus wrote unto Jonathan, saying, I confirm thee in the high priesthood, and appoint thee ruler over the four governments”. What are the four governments? Judea is one portion of them.

precepts.why:
“Wherefore we have ratified unto them the borders of Judea, with the three governments of Apherema and Lydda and Ramathem, that are added unto Judea”: that’s four, Judea, Apherema, Lydda and Ramathem. “From the country of Samaria”: these are portions of Samaria, “and all things appertaining unto them”, all the lands pertaining to Samaria, “for all such as do sacrifice in Jerusalem, instead of the payments which the king received”.

So who gained power and authority over the northern kingdom’s land? Judah, the southern kingdom, with the Levites: the Maccabees, Judas, Jonathan and Simon. Antiochus gave those lands of Samaria into our hands to govern, land which once belonged to Ephraim.

sense.text: “As concerning the rest of the acts of John”: this John is Simon’s son; write it down, this John became John Hyrcanus, the son of Simon, Judas Maccabeus’s brother. “And his wars”: he took over land. He conquered Idumea, he conquered the Arabians, and he forced Idumea to convert to Judaism when he took their land over. That’s how Herod’s family came into power, into existence. “And worthy deeds which he did, and the building of the walls which he made, and his doings”.
“Behold, these are written in the chronicles of his priesthood, from the time he was made high priest after his father.”

precepts.why:
When Antiochus defiled the temple and named it Jupiter Olympius, Judas Maccabeus and them came along, conquered the Greeks, cleansed the temple and rededicated it, and they had Hanukkah. The temple was no longer called that. But he had also set up a temple called Jupiter the Defender of strangers in Garizim, as verse two says. John Hyrcanus destroyed it: no more, you’re going to offer sacrifices in Jerusalem. That’s historical. Why? Because he gained authority over that land.

So the southern kingdom gained authority over the realms of the northern kingdom. That’s important, because now the northern kingdom could return there if they wanted, since their own people ruled over the land. That’s why Antiochus gave him the four governments and all that appertains to them, and that includes Shechem.

That’s why Ecclesiasticus said that foolish people that is no nation dwells in Shechem: remnants of Ephraim were still in the land even in his time. Ecclesiasticus was written during the time of the Greeks, write that down, so Ephraim had to have been there for him to make that statement. Remnants of them were still in the land of Shechem along with the heathens that were there.

sense.text: “Nevertheless the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation, when at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations”, when he sent Assyria against it. Zebulun and Naphtali: remember we read earlier that during Asa’s time, Hezekiah’s time and Uzziah’s time, remnants of the northern kingdom returned to Jerusalem and kept the feast. But Assyria came and took the bulk of them out of the land, like Babylon did with Judah.

“The people that walked in darkness”: because they were without a teaching priest, without law, without God. They were in idolatry based upon the sins of Jeroboam. Keep that in mind. They “have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death”, that is captivity among the heathen, “upon them hath the light shined.”

Why has the light shined on them? “For unto us a child is born”: this is the same child mentioned in Isaiah 7:14, Emmanuel. “Unto us a son is given”, given by God. That sounds very much like John 3:16: God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son. “And the government shall be upon his shoulder”: that government is the world in John 3:16. “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father”: he’s our father. “The Prince of Peace”: keep that name in mind, the Prince of Peace.

“Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end”: it shall be everlasting. “Upon the throne of David”: he will sit upon the throne of David; he’s of Judah. “To establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will perform this.” It’s prophetic.

“For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given”, and then “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it hath lighted upon Israel. And all the people shall know, even Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria”. He’s talking about Ephraim: the child that is born, the light that shined on the people that walked in darkness, is lighted upon Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria, the northern kingdom.
